events.title: Caesar's first consulship
events.summary: Backed by Pompey's veterans and Crassus' money, Caesar forced through land laws, the ratification of Pompey's eastern settlement, a one-third rebate on the Asian tax contract, a comprehensive extortion law and recognition of Ptolemy XII as king, for which Ptolemy paid Caesar and Pompey 6,000 talents. His colleague Bibulus, pelted with dung and his fasces broken, shut himself at home and declared he was watching the sky for omens, which in religious law invalidated every assembly held that year.
events.detail: Wits dated documents to the consulship of Julius and Caesar. Caesar ordered the daily publication of the proceedings of the senate (acta senatus). The religious objections to his legislation were never resolved and became the legal basis of his enemies' threat to prosecute him the moment he became a private citizen, which explains much of his conduct in 50-49. Pompey married Julia; Caesar married Calpurnia, daughter of Piso, consul for 58.
scholarship: Gelzer, Caesar: Politician and Statesman (1968)
Morstein-Marx, Julius Caesar and the Roman People (2021)
events.debate: Morstein-Marx argues Caesar acted within a defensible popular-sovereignty reading of the constitution, and that the optimates' obstruction, not Caesar's ambition, drove the crisis.

events.title: Lex Julia agraria and the Campanian law
events.summary: Caesar's first land law distributed remaining public land and land bought from willing sellers to Pompey's veterans and the poor, with a twenty-man commission; senators had to swear to obey it, and Cato and Metellus Celer gave way only at the last moment. A second law in May distributed the ager Campanus, the last great block of Italian public land, to 20,000 fathers of three or more children.

events.title: Lex Vatinia: Caesar's Gallic command
events.summary: The tribune Publius Vatinius carried a law giving Caesar Cisalpine Gaul and Illyricum for five years, to 1 March 54, with three legions. The senate, on Pompey's motion, added Transalpine Gaul and a fourth legion when its governor-designate Metellus Celer died.
events.detail: The command, extended in 55 by the lex Pompeia Licinia, was the base of all Caesar's later power. The precise terminal date of the extended command (1 March 50 or later) is one of the most debated technical problems in Roman history, because it determined when Caesar could be recalled and prosecuted.
events.debate: The 'Rechtsfrage': the legal end-date of Caesar's command (Mommsen, Balsdon, Gruen) is unresolved.

events.title: Lex Julia de repetundis
events.summary: Caesar's extortion law, over 100 chapters long, regulated governors' requisitions, gifts, and accounts, and remained the basis of Roman law on provincial misgovernment into the imperial period. Cicero called it an excellent law even while attacking its author.

events.title: The laws of Clodius: free grain and the collegia
events.summary: Publius Clodius Pulcher, a patrician who had himself adopted into a plebeian family in 59 with Caesar presiding as pontifex maximus, carried as tribune a law making the monthly grain ration free, and restored the neighbourhood associations (collegia) banned in 64. Cicero says the grain cost a fifth of state revenue.
events.detail: The collegia, organised by vicus, became the framework of Clodius' street organisation, which dominated Rome for six years. Other laws curtailed the censors' power to expel senators and restricted religious obstruction (obnuntiatio) of assemblies. Tatum argues Clodius was a popularis with his own agenda, not the triumvirs' tool.
scholarship: Tatum, The Patrician Tribune (1999)

events.title: Lex Clodia de capite civis and the exile of Cicero
events.summary: Clodius carried a law outlawing anyone who had executed a citizen without trial. Cicero, abandoned by Pompey, left Rome in March before it passed; a second law named him, banished him 400 miles and confiscated his property. His Palatine house was demolished and Clodius dedicated a shrine of Liberty on the site.
events.detail: Cicero's letters from Thessalonica and Dyrrachium are among his most despairing. The same day Clodius' laws assigned Macedonia to Piso and Syria to Gabinius, the consuls who had stood by.
events.locName: Rome; Cicero's house on the Palatine

events.title: Cato annexes Cyprus
events.summary: Clodius had Cyprus annexed from its Ptolemaic king, brother of Ptolemy XII, and sent Cato to carry out the confiscation, removing him from Rome. The king poisoned himself; Cato auctioned the royal treasures and brought back nearly 7,000 talents, keeping meticulous accounts that were then lost in a shipwreck and a fire.

events.title: Recall of Cicero
events.summary: With Pompey now hostile to Clodius, and the tribunes Milo and Sestius fighting Clodius' gangs in the streets, the centuriate assembly voted Cicero's recall. He landed at Brundisium on his daughter's birthday and entered Rome on 4 September to a hero's welcome.

events.title: Pompey takes charge of the grain supply
events.summary: Amid a grain shortage blamed on Clodius' free distributions, Cicero proposed and a consular law gave Pompey charge of the grain supply (cura annonae) for five years with proconsular imperium and 15 legates. It was another great command, and it made Pompey indispensable.

events.title: The meeting at Luca
events.summary: After meeting Crassus at Ravenna, Caesar met Pompey at Luca, the southernmost town of his province, and renewed the alliance: Pompey and Crassus would be consuls in 55 and receive five-year commands; Caesar's command would be extended. Plutarch says 200 senators and 120 lictors gathered there.
events.detail: Cicero, who had just challenged the Campanian land law, was brought to heel and delivered his recantation, the De provinciis consularibus, supporting Caesar's continued command. Whether Luca was a formal 'conference' or a series of meetings is debated; the 200 senators may be exaggerated.
scholarship: Gruen, The Last Generation of the Roman Republic (1974)

events.title: Second consulship of Pompey and Crassus; lex Trebonia
events.summary: Elected after violent delays, Pompey and Crassus had the tribune Gaius Trebonius carry a law giving Pompey both Spains and Crassus Syria for five years, and then themselves passed a law extending Caesar's Gallic command for five years. Cato, protesting, was dragged from the Forum.
events.detail: Pompey governed Spain through legates while staying near Rome, a novelty that foreshadowed the imperial system of legati Augusti.

events.title: Dedication of the Theatre of Pompey
events.summary: Pompey dedicated Rome's first permanent stone theatre, with a temple of Venus Victrix at the top of the cavea so that the seats could be described as steps to a shrine, a great portico garden, and a meeting hall (curia) in which the senate could gather. At the inaugural games 500 lions and some 18 elephants were killed.
events.detail: The elephants' cries so moved the crowd that it rose cursing Pompey, as Cicero, who found the games tasteless, reports. Caesar was killed in the curia of this complex. The theatre's curve still shapes the streets around Campo de' Fiori.

events.title: Gabinius restores Ptolemy XII
events.summary: Defying a Sibylline oracle and the senate, Aulus Gabinius, governor of Syria, marched into Egypt and restored Ptolemy XII Auletes, allegedly for 10,000 talents. His young cavalry commander Mark Antony distinguished himself at Pelusium. Gabinius was convicted of extortion in 54 and exiled; his troops, the Gabiniani, stayed in Alexandria as royal guards.

events.title: Death of Julia
events.summary: Julia, Caesar's daughter and Pompey's wife, died in childbirth in late summer 54; the child died days later. The people insisted on burying her in the Campus Martius. Ancient writers saw the loss of the personal bond between the two men as the beginning of the break; Pompey declined Caesar's offer of another marriage alliance and married Cornelia, daughter of Metellus Scipio, in 52.
events.locName: Rome; buried in the Campus Martius

events.title: Murder of Clodius and the burning of the Curia
events.summary: Clodius, riding back to Rome, met Milo's larger armed retinue on the Via Appia near Bovillae. A brawl started between the slaves; Clodius was wounded and carried into an inn, and Milo had him dragged out and killed. Next day the Clodian mob carried the body into the Curia Hostilia and cremated it on a pyre of benches and records, burning down the senate house and the Basilica Porcia.
events.detail: Asconius' commentary on Cicero's Pro Milone, using the acta, is the best narrative of any political murder in the Republic. Milo was tried in April under Pompey's new law on violence with soldiers ringing the Forum; Cicero, rattled, delivered a poor speech, and Milo went into exile at Massilia. He later said he was glad the published version had not been delivered, or he would not be enjoying the mullets of Massilia.
scholarship: Lintott, Violence in Republican Rome (1968)
Tatum, The Patrician Tribune (1999)

events.title: Pompey sole consul
events.summary: With no consuls elected for 52 and the city in chaos, the senate under a senatus consultum ultimum had Pompey named consul without a colleague, on the motion of Bibulus seconded by Cato, as the lesser evil to a dictatorship. Pompey brought in troops, passed laws on violence and bribery, and imposed a five-year gap between magistracy and provincial command.
events.detail: The tribunes' 'law of the ten', backed by Pompey, allowed Caesar to stand for the consulship in absentia; Pompey's own law on magistrates then required personal candidacy, and the exemption for Caesar was added after it had already been engraved. In August Pompey took Metellus Scipio as colleague. Ramsey and others see Pompey still balancing between Caesar and the optimates; Syme saw the move to the optimate side here.

events.title: Battle of the Arar
events.summary: The Helvetii, 368,000 people by Caesar's count, began migrating west on 28 March 58. Blocked at Geneva by Caesar's 19-mile wall along the Rhône, they took the route through Sequanian territory. Caesar caught the Tigurini canton still on the east bank of the Saône after three quarters had crossed, and cut them to pieces with three legions.
events.detail: Caesar notes with satisfaction that this canton had killed the consul Cassius and his own father-in-law's grandfather Lucius Piso in 107. He then bridged the Saône in a single day; the Helvetii, who had needed twenty to cross, sent the aged Divico to negotiate.

battle.significance: Opening blow of the Gallic Wars; justified by Caesar as both defensive and revenge for 107.

scholarship: Riggsby, Caesar in Gaul and Rome: War in Words (2006)

events.title: Battle of Bibracte
events.summary: When Caesar turned aside toward the Aeduan capital Bibracte for grain, the Helvetii attacked him. He sent away his horse and his officers', so that all shared the danger equally, and fought uphill against the Helvetian phalanx, then faced about when the Boii and Tulingi struck his flank. The fight at the wagon laager lasted into the night.
events.detail: Caesar says 130,000 survivors fled; captured Greek-script census tablets gave 368,000 emigrants, 92,000 of them warriors, and 110,000 returned home on his orders to refill the land against the Germans. The census figures, and thus the scale of the war, are among the most debated numbers in his account.

sides.losses: considerable (Caesar spent three days burying the dead)

battle.significance: Destroyed the Helvetian migration; made Caesar the arbiter of central Gaul.

events.debate: Battlefield proposed near Montmort or Armecy; Caesar's population figures are probably inflated.

events.title: Battle against Ariovistus
events.summary: Ariovistus, king of the Suebi, whom the Sequani had invited into Gaul and whom Caesar himself as consul had had declared a friend of the Roman people, now ruled much of Alsace. After a panic in the Roman camp at Vesontio, where officers made their wills, Caesar marched against him and forced a battle before the new moon that, according to captives, German seeresses said was required for victory. Publius Crassus' cavalry reserve rescued the wavering left; the Germans fled to the Rhine.
events.detail: Ariovistus escaped in a small boat; his two wives died. Caesar quelled the panic at Vesontio by saying he would march with the Tenth legion alone, the origin of its special status. The Rhine became, in Caesar's framing, the boundary between Gauls and Germans, a division that modern scholars regard partly as his construction.

sides.strength: seven peoples including Harudes, Marcomanni, Triboci, Vangiones, Nemetes, Sedusii and Suebi

battle.significance: Expelled the Suebi from Gaul and set the Rhine as Rome's de facto frontier.

events.debate: Site disputed, probably near Cernay or Mulhouse; whether Caesar's provocation was legal was challenged in Rome.

events.title: Battle of the Axona
events.summary: The Belgae, allegedly 300,000 strong, gathered against Caesar, who was guided and supplied by the Remi. Caesar fortified a camp on the Aisne with long flanking trenches and drove off Belgic attempts to cross the river. Short of food, the coalition dispersed, and the Suessiones, Bellovaci and Ambiani submitted one by one.

battle.significance: Broke up the Belgic coalition without a pitched battle.

events.title: Battle of the Sabis
events.summary: The Nervii, with the Atrebates and Viromandui, burst out of woods across the Sabis while the legions were still digging camp. The Roman army fought in disconnected blocks; the Twelfth and Seventh legions were nearly overrun, all but one centurion of the Twelfth's fourth cohort dead. Caesar snatched a shield and went to the front line; Labienus sent the Tenth back across the river and the Nervii were annihilated.
events.detail: Caesar says the Nervii reported their 600 councillors reduced to three and their 60,000 fighting men to barely 500. The senate decreed a fifteen-day thanksgiving, longer than any before. The battle is the classic instance of Caesar's 'artful reporting': the near-disaster is narrated so as to magnify the general's personal role.

battle.significance: Destroyed the most formidable Belgic people; northern Gaul submitted.

scholarship: Welch & Powell (eds), Julius Caesar as Artful Reporter (1998)

events.title: Siege of the Atuatuci
events.summary: The Atuatuci, descendants of the Cimbri and Teutones left behind in 102, laughed at Caesar's siege tower until it moved; they surrendered, threw some arms over the wall, and attacked at night with the weapons they had hidden. Caesar sold the whole population, 53,000 people by the purchasers' count.
events.detail: It is the largest single enslavement figure in Caesar's narrative, and a reminder of the slave trade's role in financing the war.

battle.significance: Completed the Belgic campaign.

events.title: Battle of Octodurus
events.summary: Servius Sulpicius Galba, sent with the Twelfth legion to open the Great St Bernard route, was attacked in his half-built winter camp at Octodurus by the Seduni and Veragri. A desperate sortie routed them, but Galba abandoned the valley.

battle.significance: Showed the Alpine route could not yet be held.

events.title: Naval battle against the Veneti
events.summary: The Veneti, the seafaring people of southern Brittany, detained Roman officers requisitioning grain. Decimus Brutus brought a fleet of galleys built on the Loire against their tall oak sailing ships with leather sails. The Romans cut the enemy halyards with sickles on poles, the wind died, and the immobilised Venetic fleet was boarded ship by ship while Caesar watched from the cliffs.
events.detail: Caesar executed the Venetic council and sold the rest of the people, on the grounds that they had violated the sanctity of envoys, though the officers were not envoys. That summer Publius Crassus conquered Aquitania, where his opponents were advised by veterans of Sertorius, and Sabinus defeated the Venelli.

sides.strength: galley fleet and Gallic allied ships

battle.significance: Rome's first Atlantic naval battle; secured Armorica and opened the Channel.

events.title: Massacre of the Usipetes and Tencteri
events.summary: Two German peoples driven from their lands by the Suebi crossed the lower Rhine, 430,000 souls by Caesar's figure. While their chiefs were in his camp negotiating, Caesar detained them and attacked the leaderless camp, slaughtering men, women and children, who were driven into the rivers. Caesar reports no Roman dead.
events.detail: In the senate Cato proposed handing Caesar over to the Germans for violating a truce, to avert divine anger. Excavations and dredged finds at Kessel on the Maas (Netherlands), with human remains, swords and spearheads of the period, have been argued since 2015 to mark the site. Caesar's figure, even if exaggerated, implies one of the largest single massacres in ancient history.
events.locName: near the confluence of the Meuse and Rhine

battle.significance: Atrocity that provoked an attempt to prosecute Caesar; ended German crossings for a time.

scholarship: Roymans, 'A Roman massacre in the far north' (2018), on Kessel

events.title: Caesar bridges the Rhine
events.summary: To show the Germans that Rome could cross at will, Caesar built a timber trestle bridge over the Rhine in ten days, describing its piles, driven at an angle against the current, and its braces in a famous technical passage. He spent eighteen days on the east bank burning Sugambrian villages and then destroyed the bridge.
events.detail: He built a second one in 53. The description has been the subject of reconstruction attempts since the Renaissance (Palladio drew one).

events.title: Caesar's first expedition to Britain
events.summary: Late in the season, with two legions, Caesar crossed from the land of the Morini. Finding armed Britons on the cliffs at Dover, he coasted to an open beach; the legionaries hesitated in the surf until the eagle-bearer of the Tenth leapt into the sea. A storm at full moon wrecked many ships, the Seventh was ambushed while foraging, and Caesar left after a few weeks with token hostages.
events.detail: The spring tide 'at full moon' (BG 4.29) has been used to date the crossing to late August 55. Archaeologists working at Ebbsfleet on Pegwell Bay have proposed that the 54 BC landing was there. In Rome the expedition beyond Ocean earned a twenty-day thanksgiving.

sides.strength: 2 legions (7th and 10th), cavalry failed to arrive

battle.significance: Propaganda triumph more than conquest: Rome's first military contact with Britain.

events.title: Second expedition to Britain: Cassivellaunus
events.summary: In 54 Caesar crossed with five legions, 2,000 cavalry and some 800 ships, beat off the British war leader Cassivellaunus' chariot tactics, forced the Thames at a staked ford and stormed his oppidum. The Trinovantes, whose prince Mandubracius had fled to Caesar, defected; Caesar imposed tribute and took hostages before a revolt in Gaul called him back.
events.detail: Caesar wrote to Cicero (Att. 4.18) that there was no silver on the island and no plunder except slaves. Quintus Cicero served on the expedition and his brother's letters follow it. Wheathampstead and other Hertfordshire sites have been proposed for the oppidum.
events.locName: Thames crossing and the oppidum of Cassivellaunus

sides.strength: allied British tribes, 4,000 charioteers kept after the main battle

battle.significance: Created the first Roman client relationships in Britain, used by Claudius in 43.

events.title: Destruction of Sabinus and Cotta at Atuatuca
events.summary: Ambiorix, king of the Eburones, persuaded Quintus Titurius Sabinus that a general Gallic rising and German invasion were coming, and offered safe passage. Overruling Lucius Aurunculeius Cotta, Sabinus marched his legion and five cohorts out of their winter camp and into an ambush in a wooded valley two miles away. Sabinus was killed while negotiating, Cotta fighting; the survivors killed themselves in the camp that night.
events.detail: The eagle-bearer Lucius Petrosidius threw the eagle inside the rampart before he died. Caesar blames Sabinus entirely and refused to cut his hair or beard until avenged. About 15 cohorts, perhaps 6,000-7,000 men, were lost: the worst Roman defeat of the Gallic Wars.

battle.significance: Triggered the rising of the Nervii and Treveri in 54-53 and Caesar's war of extermination against the Eburones.

events.title: Siege of Quintus Cicero's camp
events.summary: The Nervii and their allies besieged Quintus Cicero's legion, building a rampart and towers Roman-style and firing the thatched huts with red-hot clay sling bullets. A Gallic slave smuggled out a message; Caesar sent a letter in Greek tied to a javelin, which stuck in a tower for two days, and relieved the camp with 7,000 men, routing 60,000.
events.detail: This is the siege in which the rival centurions Titus Pullo and Lucius Vorenus each saved the other's life (BG 5.44).
events.locName: winter camp in the territory of the Nervii

battle.significance: Saved the army in northern Gaul after Atuatuca.

events.title: Battle of Carrhae
events.summary: Crassus invaded Mesopotamia with seven legions, rejecting Artavasdes of Armenia's advice to come through the hills, and was led into open steppe by the Osrhoene chieftain Abgar (Plutarch's Ariamnes). The Parthian general Surena, with 1,000 cataphracts and 9,000 horse archers resupplied with arrows from a camel train, pinned the Roman square. Publius Crassus' breakout ended with his head on a lance; the army retreated to Carrhae by night, abandoning 4,000 wounded.
events.detail: Crassus was killed at a parley a few days later. Plutarch gives 20,000 dead and 10,000 captured; the prisoners were settled at Margiana (Merv), where Horace imagines them marrying barbarian wives. Seven eagles were lost, recovered by Augustus' diplomacy in 20 BC. At the Armenian court Crassus' head was used as a prop in a performance of Euripides' Bacchae. Cassius brought out 500 horsemen and saved Syria. Ovid places the anniversary on 9 June.

battle.significance: Rome's worst defeat in the East; ended the triumvirate's balance and made Parthia Rome's great eastern rival for 270 years.

scholarship: Sampson, The Defeat of Rome: Crassus, Carrhae and the Invasion of the East (2008)
events.debate: Plutarch's narrative may draw on a Parthian-sympathetic or Cassian source; the date is uncertain, early summer 53.

events.title: Massacre at Cenabum and the rising of Vercingetorix
events.summary: The Carnutes killed the Roman traders at Cenabum, among them Caesar's grain agent Gaius Fufius Cita. The news was shouted from field to field and reached the Arverni, 160 miles away, by the end of the first watch. There the young noble Vercingetorix, expelled from Gergovia by his uncle, raised an army, was proclaimed king and became leader of a pan-Gallic rising.
events.detail: The rising exploited Caesar's absence in Cisalpine Gaul during the turmoil after Clodius' death, and anger at the execution of Acco of the Senones in 53. Caesar crossed the Cévennes through six feet of snow to reach the Arverni first.

events.title: Siege of Avaricum
events.summary: Vercingetorix ordered a scorched-earth policy, but the Bituriges begged him to spare Avaricum, their finest town. Caesar's men, starving on short rations, built a siege terrace 330 feet wide and 80 feet high in 25 days. In a rainstorm they stormed the wall; Caesar says of 40,000 inside barely 800 escaped.
events.detail: His description of the Gallic wall (murus gallicus) of timber lacing and stone facing is the classic account of the type, confirmed archaeologically at Bibracte and elsewhere.

battle.significance: Fed Caesar's army; strengthened Vercingetorix's authority, since he had urged burning the town.

events.title: Battle of Gergovia
events.summary: Caesar besieged Vercingetorix in the Arvernian hill town of Gergovia. An assault meant to seize outlying camps ran out of control up to the walls; the legionaries, deaf to the recall, were thrown back with 46 centurions and nearly 700 men killed. It was Caesar's only clear defeat by Vercingetorix, and the Aedui defected.
events.detail: Caesar blames his men's impetuosity; modern critics suspect he was trying to take the town. Excavations at the plateau and at Caesar's large and small camps confirmed the topography in the 1990s-2000s.

battle.significance: Caesar's most serious reverse in Gaul; brought the Aedui into the revolt.

scholarship: Riggsby, Caesar in Gaul and Rome (2006)

events.title: Battle of Lutetia
events.summary: Labienus, with four legions, faced the Parisii and Senones under the old commander Camulogenus near Lutetia. He crossed the Seine at night by deception, defeated Camulogenus, who was killed, and rejoined Caesar.

battle.significance: Allowed Caesar to reunite his army before Alesia.

events.title: Siege of Alesia
events.summary: After a failed cavalry attack on Caesar's column, Vercingetorix shut himself and 80,000 men in Alesia. Caesar enclosed it with a 10-mile inner line and a 14-mile outer line of ditches, ramparts, towers and booby traps, the stimuli, lilia and cippi. A relief army that Caesar puts at 250,000 foot and 8,000 horse attacked from outside while Vercingetorix attacked from within; the final assault fell on a weak camp on the north side, where Caesar himself, recognisable by his red cloak, led the reserve and German cavalry took the attackers in the rear.
events.detail: The Mandubii, the town's population, were expelled to save food, and starved between the lines when Caesar refused to let them pass. Vercingetorix surrendered the next day; later writers (Plutarch, Florus, Dio) dramatise him riding out in his finest armour and laying his arms at Caesar's feet, a scene Caesar does not describe. Each legionary received a captive as a slave. Excavations by Reddé and von Schnurbein (1991-97) confirmed the lines at Alise-Sainte-Reine against long-running claims for other sites.

sides.strength: c. 10 legions plus German cavalry and auxiliaries, perhaps 60,000-70,000
80,000 besieged; relief 250,000 foot, 8,000 horse (Caesar's figures, inflated)

battle.significance: Decided the conquest of Gaul.

scholarship: Reddé & von Schnurbein (eds), Alésia: fouilles et recherches franco-allemandes (2001)
Goldsworthy, Caesar: Life of a Colossus (2006)
events.debate: Caesar's relief-army figure is almost certainly exaggerated.

events.title: Siege of Uxellodunum
events.summary: The last Gallic holdouts under Drappes and Lucterius held the hill fort of Uxellodunum. Caesar cut off their water by tunnelling to divert the spring; the defenders, believing the gods had dried it up, surrendered. Caesar had the hands of every man who had borne arms cut off and dispersed them as a warning, his clemency being known, says Hirtius, so that the punishment would not be blamed on cruelty.
events.detail: Excavations at Puy d'Issolud found the Roman diversion tunnel and quantities of Roman arrowheads, confirming the identification.

battle.significance: Ended organised resistance in Gaul.

events.title: Caesar's Commentaries on the Gallic War
events.summary: Caesar's seven books on the Gallic War, written as plain 'notes' (commentarii) in the third person, probably drew on his annual dispatches to the senate and were in circulation by 51-50; Hirtius added an eighth. Cicero praised their unadorned elegance; Asinius Pollio thought them careless and too credulous of officers' reports and that Caesar would have revised them.
events.detail: They are the only first-person account by a Roman general of his own war to survive, and the classic case of propaganda disguised as reportage: inflated enemy numbers (368,000 Helvetii, 430,000 Usipetes and Tencteri), blame shifted to subordinates (Sabinus), omission of awkward legal issues, and silence on profits. Whether books were issued annually or all at once in 51 is debated.
scholarship: Rambaud, L'art de la déformation historique dans les Commentaires de César (1953)
Welch & Powell (eds), Julius Caesar as Artful Reporter (1998)
Riggsby, Caesar in Gaul and Rome (2006)
events.debate: Annual versus single publication; extent of deliberate distortion (Rambaud) versus conventional generalship reporting.

events.title: Parthian invasion of Syria repulsed by Cassius
events.summary: The king's son Pacorus and the general Osaces invaded Syria. Cassius, quaestor of Crassus now in charge of the province, held Antioch and ambushed the Parthians near Antigonea; Osaces was mortally wounded. Cicero, governor of neighbouring Cilicia, marched to the Taurus passes, then besieged the mountain fort of Pindenissum for 57 days and was hailed imperator.

sides.strength: Parthian army under Pacorus and Osaces

battle.significance: Saved Syria; ended the immediate Parthian threat after Carrhae.

events.title: Curio's motion: 370 votes to 22
events.summary: The tribune Gaius Scribonius Curio, whose enormous debts Caesar had quietly paid, blocked every attempt to recall Caesar unless Pompey also gave up his army. On 1 December 50 the senate voted 370 to 22 for both men to disarm. The consul Gaius Marcellus dissolved the session and, with the consuls-elect, went to Pompey and handed him a sword to defend the state.
events.detail: The vote shows that the senate as a body wanted peace; the crisis was driven by a small group around Cato, Marcellus, Lentulus and Metellus Scipio, and by Pompey's choice. Caesar argued that his dignitas and the people's grant of candidacy in absence were being stolen.
scholarship: Gruen, The Last Generation of the Roman Republic (1974)
Morstein-Marx, Julius Caesar and the Roman People (2021)

events.title: Senatus consultum ultimum against Caesar
events.summary: After Caesar's letter proposing that both commanders disarm was read on 1 January, the senate on 7 January passed the ultimate decree. The Caesarian tribunes Mark Antony and Quintus Cassius, threatened, fled to Caesar disguised as slaves, giving him a cause: the violation of tribunician sacrosanctity.

events.title: Caesar crosses the Rubicon
events.summary: With only the Thirteenth legion, 5,000 foot and 300 horse, Caesar crossed the stream marking the boundary of his province into Italy, an act of war against the state. Suetonius has him say 'iacta alea est', the die is cast; Plutarch (via Pollio) says he quoted Menander in Greek.
events.detail: Caesar's own De Bello Civili does not mention the Rubicon at all; it moves straight from his speech to the troops at Ravenna to his arrival at Ariminum. The silence is itself evidence of how carefully he managed the legal framing. The river's identity was disputed in the 18th-20th centuries; Mussolini's government officially identified it with the Fiumicino at Savignano in 1933.
scholarship: Morstein-Marx, Julius Caesar and the Roman People (2021)
events.debate: Exact date (10 or 11 January by the pre-Julian calendar; about late November 50 in Julian terms).

events.title: Siege of Corfinium
events.summary: Lucius Domitius Ahenobarbus, Caesar's designated successor in Gaul, made a stand at Corfinium with 30 cohorts against Pompey's advice. After seven days his own troops handed him over. Caesar released Domitius and the senators with him and enrolled the soldiers, proclaiming a new way of conquering by mercy and generosity.
events.detail: Domitius had tried to poison himself, but his doctor gave him a sleeping draught. Caesar's letter about his clemency survives in Cicero's correspondence (Att. 9.7C). Domitius promptly went to hold Massilia against him.

sides.strength: 6 legions by the end of the siege

battle.significance: Showcase of clementia; Pompey abandoned Italy.

events.title: Pompey abandons Italy
events.summary: Pompey shipped his army from Brundisium to Dyrrachium, slipping out on 17 March despite Caesar's attempt to close the harbour mouth with moles and rafts. His strategy was to gather the resources of the East and starve Italy; Cicero thought it a Sullan plan and was appalled.

events.title: Caesar takes the treasury
events.summary: In Rome Caesar forced open the state treasury in the temple of Saturn, including the sacred reserve kept against Gallic invasion, which he declared obsolete since he had conquered the Gauls. When the tribune Lucius Metellus barred the way, Caesar told him it was harder to say than to do that he would kill him.
events.detail: Pliny gives 15,000 gold bars, 30,000 silver bars and 30 million sesterces in coin. Caesar's De Bello Civili omits the episode.

events.title: Siege of Massilia
events.summary: Massilia shut its gates to Caesar and admitted Domitius Ahenobarbus. Gaius Trebonius besieged it by land with a huge terrace and a six-storey brick tower, while Decimus Brutus' hastily built fleet won two naval battles. Starving and plague-stricken, the city surrendered when Caesar returned from Spain; it kept nominal freedom but lost its fleet, treasury and most of its territory.

battle.significance: Ended Massilia's independent power, six centuries old.

events.title: Campaign of Ilerda
events.summary: Pompey's legates Afranius and Petreius held Ilerda with five legions and many auxiliaries. A flood swept away Caesar's bridges over the Sicoris and nearly starved him; he built light coracles like those he had seen in Britain and restored his communications. When the Pompeians tried to slip away to the Ebro, Caesar headed them off, cut them from water and forced their surrender without a pitched battle on 2 August.
events.detail: He discharged them, a stroke of clemency and economy. Varro then surrendered Further Spain. Caesar said he was going to Spain to fight an army without a general, and then East to fight a general without an army.

sides.losses: c. 70 in the worst skirmish; light overall

sides.strength: 5 legions and c. 80 cohorts of Spanish auxiliaries under Afranius and Petreius

battle.significance: Secured the West for Caesar within six months of the Rubicon.

scholarship: Goldsworthy, Caesar: Life of a Colossus (2006)

events.title: Battle of the Bagradas: death of Curio
events.summary: Curio, sent to seize Africa with legions that had surrendered at Corfinium, beat the Pompeian Attius Varus near Utica, then, deceived by a report that King Juba had withdrawn, rushed his tired army into the ambush of Juba's general Saburra on the Bagradas. Curio refused to escape, saying he could not face Caesar having lost the army entrusted to him, and died fighting.
events.detail: Caesar's account is unusually generous to a subordinate and reads as a eulogy. Juba killed many of the prisoners against Varus' wishes.

sides.strength: Numidian cavalry and infantry under Saburra

battle.significance: Left Africa in Pompeian hands until 46.

events.title: Caesar's first dictatorship and the enfranchisement of the Transpadanes
events.summary: Named dictator to hold elections, Caesar held office for eleven days in late 49, had himself elected consul for 48, eased debts by valuing property at pre-war prices, recalled most exiles except Milo, and gave citizenship to the Transpadanes (lex Roscia), completing the enfranchisement of Italy to the Alps.

events.title: Battle of Dyrrhachium
events.summary: Caesar, having crossed in January past Bibulus' fleet and been joined by Antony in April, tried to blockade Pompey's larger army against the sea with 17 miles of earthworks. His men ate bread made from a root called chara; the centurion Scaeva's shield took 120 holes holding a fort. Informed by two Allobrogian deserters of a gap at the southern end, Pompey broke through; Caesar's counterattack collapsed in panic and he lost 960 men and 32 officers.
events.detail: Caesar said that the war would have been lost that day if the enemy had had a commander who knew how to win. Pompey did not pursue. Caesar retreated into Thessaly and Pompey, urged by his senatorial staff to finish the war, followed.

battle.significance: Pompey's victory broke the blockade but his failure to pursue let Caesar regroup.

events.title: Battle of Pharsalus
events.summary: Pompey, with about 45,000 infantry and 7,000 cavalry, planned for Labienus' massed cavalry to sweep around Caesar's right while his infantry stood still to receive the charge. Caesar, with 22,000 infantry and 1,000 cavalry, had secretly formed a fourth line of six cohorts behind his right, which routed the cavalry, thrusting their pila at the riders' faces, and then rolled up Pompey's left. Pompey left the field for his camp and then fled.
events.detail: Caesar claims 15,000 Pompeians killed and 24,000 captured against 200 men and 30 centurions of his own; Asinius Pollio, who was there, gave 6,000 dead. Domitius Ahenobarbus was killed in flight; Brutus was pardoned. Pollio reported Caesar's words over the dead: 'They wanted it'. The date is 9 August by the unreformed calendar, about 7 June or later in Julian terms. The battlefield (north or south of the Enipeus) is disputed.
events.locName: plain of Pharsalus, near the Enipeus, Thessaly

battle.significance: Decided the civil war in the East; the old senatorial government never recovered.

scholarship: Goldsworthy, Caesar: Life of a Colossus (2006)
Gelzer, Caesar: Politician and Statesman (1968)
events.debate: Battlefield location; Caesar's numbers (especially Pompeian losses) versus Pollio's.

events.title: Murder of Pompey at Pelusium
events.summary: Pompey sought refuge with the court of Ptolemy XIII, whose father he had helped restore. The king's advisers Pothinus, Achillas and Theodotus decided a dead Pompey was safer; as he was rowed ashore he was stabbed by Achillas and the former Roman centurion Lucius Septimius in sight of his wife Cornelia. He was killed on or about the eve of his 58th birthday.
events.detail: His freedman Philippus burned the headless body on the beach with the timbers of a fishing boat. When Caesar arrived at Alexandria days later, Theodotus presented him with the head and signet ring; Caesar wept, or performed weeping. The Psalms of Solomon and Lucan both meditate on the great man unburied on the Egyptian shore.

events.title: The Alexandrian War: Caesar besieged in the palace
events.summary: Caesar, with only 3,200 infantry and 800 cavalry, tried to arbitrate between Ptolemy XIII and his sister Cleopatra VII, who had herself smuggled into the palace. The king's general Achillas and then Arsinoe's eunuch Ganymedes besieged him in the royal quarter for months; Ganymedes pumped seawater into the palace cisterns, and in a fight on the Pharos causeway Caesar had to swim for it, holding his papers above the water.
events.detail: To stop the Egyptian fleet he burned the ships in the harbour; the fire spread to dockside warehouses. Seneca, citing Livy, says 40,000 books burned; Plutarch and Dio speak of the great library or of book stores. Most scholars think warehouses of books near the harbour, not the Museum's main library, were destroyed; the Library continued to function in some form.

sides.losses: considerable; 400 killed at the Pharos mole alone

sides.strength: c. 20,000 under Achillas incl. the Gabiniani

battle.significance: Put Cleopatra on the throne; delayed Caesar's return for nine months while the Pompeians regrouped in Africa.

scholarship: Roller, Cleopatra (2010)
events.debate: Extent of damage to the Library of Alexandria.

events.title: Battle of Nicopolis
events.summary: Pharnaces II, son of Mithridates, exploited the civil war to reconquer Pontus. Caesar's legate Gnaeus Domitius Calvinus, with one Roman legion, a scratch legion from Pontus and Deiotarus' two legions trained in the Roman manner, was defeated near Nicopolis.

battle.significance: Gave Pharnaces Pontus and drew Caesar to Asia in 47.

events.title: Battle of the Nile
events.summary: Relieved by an army of Syrian and Jewish allies under Mithridates of Pergamon and Antipater, Caesar marched up the Delta and stormed Ptolemy XIII's fortified camp. The young king drowned when his overloaded boat sank; his body was identified by his golden armour. Alexandria surrendered and Cleopatra was made queen with her younger brother Ptolemy XIV.
events.detail: Caesar then spent weeks on a Nile cruise with Cleopatra, according to Suetonius nearly to Ethiopia. Antipater was rewarded with Roman citizenship and his son Herod's career began. A son, Ptolemy Caesar (Caesarion), was born in 47, whose paternity became political dynamite.

sides.strength: Caesar's legions plus Mithridates of Pergamon's relief army

battle.significance: Ended the Alexandrian War.

events.title: Battle of Zela: veni, vidi, vici
events.summary: Five days after arriving, while his men were entrenching on a hill facing Pharnaces' position, Caesar was attacked uphill by the king's army with scythed chariots. The veteran Sixth legion, reduced to under 1,000 men, broke the attack on the right and the Pontic army was routed within four hours.
events.detail: Caesar summed it up in a letter to his friend Matius, Plutarch says, or on a placard in his Pontic triumph, Suetonius says: 'veni, vidi, vici'. He also remarked on Pompey's luck in having won his name against such enemies. Pharnaces fled to the Bosporus and was killed by his rebel governor Asander.

battle.significance: Restored Roman control of Asia Minor in a single afternoon.

events.title: Mutiny of the Tenth legion
events.summary: Veterans in Campania, led by the Tenth, mutinied demanding discharge and their promised rewards, killed two ex-praetors sent to them and marched on Rome. Caesar faced them in the Campus Martius, granted discharge at once and addressed them as 'Quirites', citizens, instead of soldiers. Shamed, they begged to be taken to Africa.
events.detail: That same year Dolabella's agitation for debt cancellation led to street fighting in Rome that Antony, as master of horse, suppressed with troops.

events.title: Battle of Ruspina
events.summary: Landing in Africa with only part of his army, Caesar (who stumbled on the beach and turned it into an omen with 'I hold you, Africa') was caught foraging near Ruspina by Labienus' Numidian cavalry and light infantry and surrounded. He extended his line and had alternate cohorts face about, broke out and fell back to camp at nightfall as Petreius arrived.

sides.strength: Numidian cavalry and light infantry, c. 10,000+

battle.significance: Caesar narrowly escaped disaster in the first weeks of the African campaign.

events.title: Battle of Thapsus
events.summary: Caesar besieged Thapsus to force Metellus Scipio and King Juba to battle on a narrow strip between lagoon and sea. Before he gave the signal his veterans charged; slingers and archers stampeded Scipio's elephants, which the Fifth legion met on foot, and the Pompeian army collapsed. Caesar's soldiers butchered men trying to surrender.
events.detail: The anonymous Bellum Africum says Caesar lost 50 men and the enemy 10,000; Plutarch claims 50,000 enemy dead and reports a story that Caesar suffered an epileptic seizure as the battle began. The Fifth (Alaudae) took the elephant as its emblem.

sides.strength: c. 10 legions with veterans of the 5th, 9th, 10th, 13th and 14th
c. 10 Roman legions, Numidian forces, 60 elephants

battle.significance: Destroyed the Pompeian army in Africa; Numidia annexed as Africa Nova.

events.title: Suicide of Cato at Utica
events.summary: Commanding Utica, Cato organised the escape of those who wished to flee, refused to seek Caesar's pardon, read Plato's Phaedo on the immortality of the soul twice, and stabbed himself. His physicians bandaged the wound; when he came to, he tore it open and died.
events.detail: Caesar is said to have exclaimed that he begrudged Cato his death, as Cato had begrudged him the chance to save his life. Cato's death made him the martyr of republican liberty: Cicero wrote a eulogy (Cato), Caesar replied with an Anticato, and Lucan and Seneca made him a Stoic saint. Juba and Petreius killed each other in a duel; Metellus Scipio stabbed himself at sea, telling his captors that the commander was well.

events.title: Caesar's quadruple triumph
events.summary: Caesar celebrated four triumphs within a month, over Gaul, Egypt, Pontus and Africa (officially over Juba). Vercingetorix, held six years, was executed afterwards; Arsinoe, Cleopatra's sister, was paraded but spared; the infant Juba II walked in the procession. His soldiers sang that Caesar had subdued the Gauls and Nicomedes had subdued Caesar, and warned citizens to lock up their wives because the bald adulterer was back.
events.detail: Each veteran received 24,000 sesterces; each citizen 400 sesterces, grain and oil. The games included a mock naval battle in a basin dug on the Campus Martius and the first giraffe seen in Rome. A census of grain recipients cut the dole from 320,000 to 150,000. On 26 September Caesar dedicated his new Forum with the temple of Venus Genetrix, in which he set a golden statue of Cleopatra.

events.title: The Julian calendar
events.summary: As pontifex maximus Caesar, advised by the Alexandrian astronomer Sosigenes, replaced the lunisolar Republican calendar, which through neglected intercalation had drifted nearly three months ahead of the seasons, with a solar year of 365 days and a leap day every fourth year. To realign it, 46 was given 445 days, adding an intercalary month after February and two extra months between November and December; the new calendar began on 1 January 45.
events.detail: Macrobius and Censorinus call 46 the last year of confusion. The pontiffs then misapplied the rule, intercalating every third year, until Augustus suspended leap years from 9 BC and restored the cycle from AD 8. With the Gregorian adjustment of 1582 it remains the world's civil calendar. Cicero, told that the constellation Lyra would rise the next day, quipped that it was doing so by edict.
scholarship: Feeney, Caesar's Calendar (2007)

events.title: Caesar's colonies and the refoundation of Carthage and Corinth
events.summary: Caesar settled some 80,000 citizens, veterans and urban poor, in colonies overseas, including refoundations of Corinth (Laus Iulia Corinthiensis) and Carthage, both destroyed in 146, and Urso in Spain, whose charter (lex coloniae Genetivae Iuliae) survives on bronze tablets. Freedmen were allowed to hold office in some colonies.

events.title: Battle of Munda
events.summary: In Spain Pompey's sons Gnaeus and Sextus and Labienus raised 13 legions. At Munda they took a strong hillside position; Caesar attacked and for hours the issue hung in the balance, Caesar saying afterwards that he had often fought for victory but this time for his life. When Bogud of Mauretania's cavalry threatened the Pompeian camp, Labienus pulled five cohorts back to cover it; the movement was taken for retreat and the line broke.
events.detail: The Bellum Hispaniense claims 30,000 Pompeian dead, including Labienus and Attius Varus, against 1,000 Caesarian. The Caesarians walled the town with corpses, shields and javelins, with heads on swords facing the defenders. Gnaeus was hunted down and killed weeks later; Sextus escaped. Caesar's triumph over Roman citizens in October offended many. The battlefield's location (near Osuna or Montilla) is disputed; recent finds near La Lantejuela and Osuna favour the Osuna area.

battle.significance: Last major battle of Caesar's civil war.

events.title: Caesar dictator for life
events.summary: Already dictator for ten years from 46, by mid-February 44 Caesar took the title dictator perpetuo, struck on coins (RRC 480). Honours piled up: the title parens patriae, a statue among the kings on the Capitol, a gilded chair, the renaming of Quinctilis as Iulius, a temple to his Clemency, and a flamen of his own. When the senate came to him at the temple of Venus Genetrix, he did not rise.
events.detail: When tribunes removed a diadem placed on his statue and arrested a man who hailed him as king, Caesar had them deposed. He joked that he was not Rex but Caesar. The perpetual dictatorship closed any prospect of a return to normal government and was the decisive provocation for the conspiracy.
scholarship: Morstein-Marx, Julius Caesar and the Roman People (2021)

events.title: The Lupercalia: Antony offers Caesar a diadem
events.summary: At the Lupercalia the consul Mark Antony, running near-naked as a Lupercus, offered Caesar, seated on the Rostra in triumphal dress, a royal diadem. Caesar refused it; the crowd cheered; Antony offered it again, and again it was refused, and Caesar had it sent to Jupiter on the Capitol. The fasti were made to record that the consul had offered kingship at the people's bidding and Caesar had refused.
events.detail: Whether it was a staged test of opinion, a demonstration that Caesar did not want kingship, or Antony's own initiative was debated then and now. Cicero's Second Philippic makes the most of it.

events.title: The Ides of March: assassination of Caesar
events.summary: Three days before he was to leave for a war against Parthia with 16 legions and 10,000 cavalry, Caesar was stabbed to death at a meeting of the senate in the curia of Pompey's theatre complex by more than 60 conspirators led by Marcus Brutus, Gaius Cassius and Decimus Brutus. Trebonius detained Antony outside; Tillius Cimber pulled at Caesar's toga; Casca struck first. He received 23 wounds, of which, his physician judged, only the second, in the chest, was fatal, and fell at the foot of Pompey's statue.
events.detail: The haruspex Spurinna had warned him of danger lasting until the Ides; Calpurnia dreamed of holding his bloody body. Suetonius records, and doubts, the story that he said in Greek to Brutus, 'You too, child?' Most sources say he died silent, pulling his toga over his head. The conspirators, calling themselves liberators, had no plan for what followed; Brutus vetoed killing Antony. Brutus' later coin showing a cap of liberty between two daggers and EID MAR (RRC 508/3) is the most famous Roman coin. The curia's remains lie behind Temple B in the Largo Argentina.
scholarship: Strauss, The Death of Caesar (2015)
Tempest, Brutus: The Noble Conspirator (2017)
Syme, The Roman Revolution (1939)
events.debate: Whether the assassination was a principled defence of republican liberty, an aristocratic reaction against a popular leader (Morstein-Marx), or factional resentment; Nicolaus of Damascus is the earliest narrative, from Augustus' court.
